newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish lower house passes draft banking law.
newsitem.headline: Polish lower house passes draft banking law.

text.p: Poland's lower house of parliament on Friday approved a draft banking law designed to enhance the security of the banking system and upgrade it to European Union standards.

The bill, passed in a 342 to six vote with five abstentions, provides for creating an independent Banking Supervision Commission that would oversee the sector and guard against unfair competition between banks.

It now must clear the senate and be signed by the president. The bill also aims to regulate more closely the origins of banks' capital and their ownership structures, preventing the expansion of "internal" loans -- meaning credits extended to subsidiaries shareholders and employers -- and helping to protect against money laundering.
The National Bank of Poland (NBP), which helped draft the bill, said it would help accumulate savings, which could in the future be used to finance the country's economic growth.

Among the bill's provisions is a ban on banks tying up more than 15 percent of their own funds -- comprising statutory funds, share capital and reserves -- to buy shares of companies that are not banks. However, they would be allowed to extend credits worth up to 25 percent of their own funds to a single entity.

Any purchaser of a bank's shares representing five percent or more shareholders' votes would have to report the move to the new Banking Supervision Commission, which would also have to agree further purchases boosting voting share.
The bill also stipulates that electronic data be treated as legally binding.

Last month Finance Minister Marek Belka said he hoped legislators would pass the bill before general elections due around September, or a new government and parliament might start work afresh, further delaying its passage.
